fish.text: Before collecting requirements, find the real problem. The fishbone, or Ishikawa, diagram puts the problem at the head, on the right.

bones.text: Four to eight main causes become the bones. Sub-causes attach to them, often from a brainstorming session. The goal: the root cause.

research.text: Research: journals, books, and websites of similar projects.

observe.text: Observation: watch people at work. The data is very reliable, but people may act differently when watched.

proto.text: Prototyping: a small working model for users to try. But users may develop unrealistic expectations.

question.text: Questionnaires: cheap, anonymous, and fast for many people. Open-ended questions let people answer freely. Closed-ended ones offer fixed choices. The downside: a low return rate.

interview.text: Interviews: face to face. Unstructured, with only a general goal, or structured, with a fixed set of questions. Rich, but time-consuming.

sample.text: Sampling collects representative documents and forms. Random sampling picks by pure chance. Systematic sampling picks every x over n-th: one hundred from a thousand means every tenth. Stratified sampling splits into subgroups first.

jrp.text: And Joint Requirements Planning: a workshop of users, managers and I T staff, led by a facilitator, with a sponsor from top management.
